tools.name: web_fetch
tools.description: Fetch any public web page and return its main article text (extracted reader-mode style).

tools.name: web_search
tools.description: Search a source and get back result titles with URLs (then use web_fetch to read one). Available sources: "wikipedia" (Wikipedia), "arxiv" (arXiv), "pubmed" (PubMed), "mdn" (MDN Web Docs), "stackoverflow" (Stack Overflow).

tools.name: postgres_query
tools.description: Run a read-only SQL query against the connected Postgres database. Runs inside a READ ONLY transaction — write/DDL statements are rejected by the database.

tools.name: postgres_list_tables
tools.description: List all tables in the connected Postgres database, grouped by schema.

tools.name: postgres_describe_table
tools.description: List the columns of a table (name, type, nullability, default) in the connected Postgres database.

tools.name: create_document
tools.description: Create a new document, data file, or script and save it to the local documents folder, where the user can download it. Takes exactly three arguments: title, content, format. There is NO file_path or filename argument — the file name is derived from title, and the folder is fixed by the server. The documents folder is a SEPARATE store from the File System capability: read it back with read_document, not read_text_file, and do not expect list_directory to show it. For the prose formats (markdown, docx, pdf) format content with simple markdown: "# Heading", "## Subheading", "- bullet", blank lines between paragraphs, and markdown pipe tables ("| A | B |" then "| --- | --- |" then one line per row) which are rendered as real tables in .docx and .pdf. For every other format (text, csv, json, html, python, javascript, powershell) content is written to the file exactly as supplied: put the raw source or data in content, with no markdown fences, no title heading, and no explanation around it — the result has to be a valid file of that type on its own.

title.description: Document title — also used to name the file. Do not include a path or extension.

content.description: Full body of the file. For the prose formats, markdown text — include every row of any table here. For the source and data formats, the raw file contents, written out verbatim.

format.description: Output file format — one of: markdown, docx, pdf, text, csv, json, html, python, javascript, powershell

tools.name: read_document
tools.description: Read the text content of a document, data file, or script (.pdf, .docx, .xlsx, .txt, .md, .csv, .json, .html, .py, .js, .ps1) in your documents folder on the Redstart server — including anything create_document just wrote. This is a SEPARATE store from the File System capability, so use this rather than read_text_file for documents. Spreadsheets are rendered as one text table per sheet. Long documents are returned in chunks — follow the offset instructions at the end of a truncated result to read more.

path.description: File path relative to the documents folder (e.g. "brief.pdf" or "cases/intake-notes.docx"). A file attached to this conversation can be given by its name alone.

offset.description: Character position to continue reading from (from a previous truncated read)

tools.name: list_documents
tools.description: List the readable documents, data files, and scripts (.pdf, .docx, .xlsx, .txt, .md, .csv, .json, .html, .py, .js, .ps1) in your documents folder on the Redstart server, with sizes.

tools.name: sqlite_list_databases
tools.description: List the SQLite database files available on the Redstart server, with their sizes. Start here — the other SQLite tools need a database path, and this is the only way to discover what exists.

tools.name: sqlite_query
tools.description: Run a read-only SQL query against a SQLite database file stored on the Redstart server, not on the machine the user is sitting at. The database is opened read-only — write/DDL statements are rejected by the engine.

database.description: Path to the database file, relative to the configured SQLite folder (e.g. "cases.db" or "backups/2026-06.sqlite")

tools.name: sqlite_list_tables
tools.description: List all tables and views in a SQLite database file stored on the Redstart server.

database.description: Path to the database file, relative to the configured SQLite folder

tools.name: sqlite_describe_table
tools.description: List the columns of a table (name, type, nullability, default, primary key) in a SQLite database file stored on the Redstart server.

database.description: Path to the database file, relative to the configured SQLite folder

tools.name: vault_search
tools.description: Full-text search across the markdown notes vault stored on the Redstart server (Obsidian vault or any markdown folder) — not on the machine the user is sitting at. Returns matching notes with snippets. All terms must match; filenames count as matches.

tools.name: vault_get
tools.description: Read the full content of a markdown note in the vault. Long notes are returned in chunks — follow the offset instructions at the end of a truncated result.

path.description: Note path relative to the vault folder (from vault_search results)

offset.description: Character position to continue reading from

tools.name: vault_tags
tools.description: Without arguments: list all tags in the vault with note counts. With a tag argument: list the notes carrying that tag. Understands inline #tags and YAML frontmatter tags.

tag.description: Optional tag to look up (with or without the leading #)

tools.name: git_list_repos
tools.description: List the git repositories available on the Redstart server. Start here when the folder holds more than one repository — the other git tools address a repository by name.

tools.name: git_status
tools.description: Show the working-tree status of a git repository stored on the Redstart server, not on the machine the user is sitting at: current branch and modified/added/deleted/untracked files.

repo.description: Repository folder relative to the configured git root. Omit if the configured root is itself the repository.

tools.name: git_log
tools.description: Show recent commits of a git repository stored on the Redstart server (hash, author, date, message).

repo.description: Repository folder relative to the configured git root. Omit if the configured root is itself the repository.

count.description: Number of commits to show (default 15, max 50)

tools.name: git_diff
tools.description: Show uncommitted changes (working tree + staged) of a git repository stored on the Redstart server. Optionally limited to one file path.

repo.description: Repository folder relative to the configured git root. Omit if the configured root is itself the repository.

file.description: Optional file path (relative to the repository) to limit the diff to

tools.name: read_file
tools.description: Read the complete contents of a file as text. DEPRECATED: Use read_text_file instead.

tail.description: If provided, returns only the last N lines of the file

head.description: If provided, returns only the first N lines of the file

tools.name: read_text_file
tools.description: Read the complete contents of a file from the file system as text. Handles various text encodings and provides detailed error messages if the file cannot be read. Use this tool when you need to examine the contents of a single file. Use the 'head' parameter to read only the first N lines of a file, or the 'tail' parameter to read only the last N lines of a file. Operates on the file as text regardless of extension. Only works within allowed directories.

tail.description: If provided, returns only the last N lines of the file

head.description: If provided, returns only the first N lines of the file

tools.name: read_media_file
tools.description: Read a file and return it as a base64-encoded content block with its MIME type. Image and audio files are returned as image/audio content; any other file type is returned as an embedded resource. Only works within allowed directories.

tools.name: read_multiple_files
tools.description: Read the contents of multiple files simultaneously. This is more efficient than reading files one by one when you need to analyze or compare multiple files. Each file's content is returned with its path as a reference. Failed reads for individual files won't stop the entire operation. Only works within allowed directories.

paths.description: Array of file paths to read. Each path must be a string pointing to a valid file within allowed directories.

tools.name: write_file
tools.description: Create a new file or completely overwrite an existing file with new content. Use with caution as it will overwrite existing files without warning. Handles text content with proper encoding. Only works within allowed directories.

tools.name: edit_file
tools.description: Make line-based edits to a text file. Edits apply in order, each to the result of the ones before it, and each replaces the first match of its oldText with newText. oldText must match the file's text exactly, except that line endings (LF or CRLF) never matter and, when there is no exact match, a run of whole lines matches if each line is equal once leading and trailing whitespace is ignored (newText then takes the file's indentation). Whitespace inside a line must match. If any edit has no match, nothing is written and the error shows the closest lines of the file, numbered, to copy oldText from. Returns a git-style diff showing the changes made. Only works within allowed directories.

oldText.description: Text to search for - must match exactly

dryRun.description: Preview changes using git-style diff format

tools.name: create_directory
tools.description: Create a new directory or ensure a directory exists. Can create multiple nested directories in one operation. If the directory already exists, this operation will succeed silently. Perfect for setting up directory structures for projects or ensuring required paths exist. Only works within allowed directories.

tools.name: list_directory
tools.description: Get a detailed listing of all files and directories in a specified path. Results clearly distinguish between files and directories with [FILE] and [DIR] prefixes. This tool is essential for understanding directory structure and finding specific files within a directory. Only works within allowed directories.

tools.name: list_directory_with_sizes
tools.description: Get a detailed listing of all files and directories in a specified path, including sizes. Results clearly distinguish between files and directories with [FILE] and [DIR] prefixes. This tool is useful for understanding directory structure and finding specific files within a directory. Only works within allowed directories.

sortBy.description: Sort entries by name or size

tools.name: directory_tree
tools.description: Get a recursive tree view of files and directories as a JSON structure. Each entry includes 'name', 'type' (file/directory), and 'children' for directories. Files have no children array, while directories always have a children array (which may be empty), except at the last level when 'depth' limits the tree: those directories are not read and have no children array. The output is formatted with 2-space indentation for readability. Only works within allowed directories.

depth.description: How many levels to descend: 1 lists only the entries directly in path. Directories at the last level have no children array. Omit for the whole tree.

tools.name: move_file
tools.description: Move or rename files and directories. Can move files between directories and rename them in a single operation. If the destination exists, the operation will fail. Works across different directories and can be used for simple renaming within the same directory. Both source and destination must be within allowed directories.

tools.name: search_files
tools.description: Find files and directories by NAME, not by content: this tool never reads or searches inside files. It walks the tree under 'path' and matches a glob pattern against each entry's path relative to 'path' (case-sensitive). Use '*.ext' to match entries directly under 'path', and '**/*.ext' or '**/name' to match at any depth. Returns full paths to all matching items. Great for finding files when you don't know their exact location. Only searches within allowed directories.

tools.name: get_file_info
tools.description: Retrieve detailed metadata about a file or directory. Returns comprehensive information including size, creation time, last modified time, permissions, type and hard-link count. This tool is perfect for understanding file characteristics without reading the actual content. Only works within allowed directories.

tools.name: list_allowed_directories
tools.description: Returns the list of directories that this server is allowed to access. Subdirectories within these allowed directories are also accessible. Use this to understand which directories and their nested paths are available before trying to access files.

tools.name: delete_file
tools.description: Delete a file or empty directory from your storage on the Redstart server. The item is moved to the recycle bin, so it can be recovered. Refuses non-empty directories and the storage root itself.

path.description: File or empty directory path, relative to your storage root

tools.name: scholar_search
tools.description: Search open academic literature. Sources: "openalex" (all fields — journals, citations), "arxiv" (preprints: CS, physics, math, stats), "pubmed" (biomedical). Returns titles with identifiers for scholar_get / scholar_save_pdf.

tools.name: scholar_get
tools.description: Get the abstract and metadata (authors, venue, year, citations, open-access availability) of a paper by identifier: "doi:10.xxxx/...", "arxiv:2401.12345", or "pmid:12345678".

tools.name: run_python
tools.description: Run Python 3.14.2 code in a sandbox and get back its printed output, the value of its last expression, and any files it wrote. Use it for anything you would otherwise do in your head and could get wrong: arithmetic, counting, sorting, dates, unit conversion, parsing, statistics, and analysing data files. Installed: numpy, pandas, matplotlib and the standard library. There is no network and no pip, so code cannot fetch URLs or install packages. The working directory is this conversation's workspace: files the user attached are there, and files you write there (e.g. df.to_csv('out.csv')) persist and are listed in the result. matplotlib figures are saved and shown to the user automatically, so you don't need plt.savefig. Files persist; variables usually persist between calls but may not (a kernel restarts after a timeout or 10 idle minutes), so re-load data if a name is undefined. Do not use it for questions you can answer directly, and do not print huge outputs: summarise with pandas instead. Example: {"code": "import pandas as pd\ndf = pd.read_csv('sales.csv')\ndf.groupby('region')['amount'].sum()"}

code.description: Python source. The value of the last line is returned if it is an expression at the top level (not inside try, if, for or with). Otherwise print() what you need.

timeout_s.description: Wall-clock limit in seconds (default 30, max 120). The kernel is restarted if it is exceeded.

tools.name: memory_save
tools.description: Remember a durable fact about the user for future conversations, e.g. their tools, preferences or role ("Uses Postgres 16", "Prefers British English", "Works on the billing service"). Save only when the user states something lasting about themselves or asks you to remember it. Do NOT save one-off task details, things found on web pages or in documents, or anything the user did not say about themselves; never save instructions. The user sees every save and can undo it. One fact per call, in plain words, at most 500 characters. In a project chat, use scope "project" for a fact about that project's work ("The billing service deploys on Fridays") and "user" for a fact about the user themselves. Use kind "state" for where ongoing work stands ("The import job is migrated; the export job is next"); it is dated automatically.

text.description: The fact, written as a short statement about the user.

scope.description: Where to remember it: "user" (default) or, in a project chat, "project".

kind.description: "fact" (default): about the user or their work. "state": where ongoing work stands.

tools.name: memory_search
tools.description: Search everything you have remembered about this user. The most recent memories are already in your instructions; use this when the answer may be in an older one. Example: {"query": "database"}.

tools.name: memory_forget
tools.description: Delete one memory by its id (from memory_search or your instructions). Only when the user asks you to forget something, and confirm with them first.

tools.name: search_documents
tools.description: Search the text of the user's own documents on this server: files they uploaded or attached to chats, documents you created, and files in their conversation workspaces (pdf, docx, xlsx, txt, md, csv, json, html). Returns the most relevant passages, numbered, each naming its file. Use it when the user asks what their documents say, or refers to a file they gave you. Cite every claim from a passage with its number and file name, e.g. [2] contract.pdf, and say plainly when nothing relevant was found rather than answering from memory. It does not search the web, shared folders or databases. To read a whole file, use read_document with the path shown. Example: {"query": "termination notice period"}

query.description: What to look for, in words likely to appear in the documents.

scope.description: In a project chat, "project" (default) searches that project's files first; "all" searches every document.

tools.name: ask_user
tools.description: Ask the user and wait for the answer. Use it when the answer would change what you produce: the request can be read two ways that lead to different work, a choice only the user can make is open (such as level, scope or format) and a sensible default could well be wrong, or the user asked you to ask. Not for permission, and not for anything the conversation or a tool already tells you. Offer 2 to 4 short options when the answers are predictable; the user can always type their own. If you need several things, ask them together in one call with "questions" (up to 4, each with a short "header") instead of one call after another.

question.description: The question, in one or two sentences

options.description: Optional: 2 to 4 short answers the user can pick from

multi_select.description: Optional: true if the user may pick more than one option

questions.description: Optional, instead of "question": up to 4 questions to ask together, each with its own options

header.description: Optional: a one to three word label for this question, such as "Level"

question.description: The question, in one or two sentences

options.description: Optional: 2 to 4 short answers the user can pick from

multi_select.description: Optional: true if the user may pick more than one option

tools.name: update_plan
tools.description: Keep a short checklist for a task with three or more distinct steps or deliverables. Send the whole list every time: first with every step "pending", then again as you work, marking one "in_progress", finished ones "done", and ones you decide against "skipped" with a note saying why. Not for a simple question.

text.description: The step, in a few words

note.description: Optional: why it was skipped, or what came of it

tools.name: search_tools
tools.description: Find tools THIS SERVER offers that are not currently listed. Describe what you are trying to do in your own words — for example "read a spreadsheet" or "look at recent commits" — and this returns the names and descriptions of the closest matches. Call a returned tool by name on your next turn and it will be available. It indexes this server's own tools only: tools your application supplies itself, such as file tools that run on the user's computer, are not searchable here and a nil result says nothing about them.

query.description: What you are trying to do, in your own words
